capabilities.title: Verified simplification
capabilities.summary: Searches a short chain of rewrites toward a goal (simplify, expand, factor, or rewrite in given functions): handbook identities, each at every place it matches and read in either direction, plus SymPy's own moves. Every step is checked at random complex sample points and, separately, with a symbolic zero test; the steps and the identities used are shown. A result that cannot be verified is never shown.
limits: Numerical agreement at sample points is evidence, not proof; only a passed symbolic zero test means SymPy also reduced the difference to zero. Both are reported for every step.

Steps are equalities where both sides are defined. When the result excludes points the input did not (a cancelled factor), it says where it is valid (`x \neq 1`); square-root, logarithm and branch-cut domains are not reported this way.
The search is bounded (at most 4 rewrites in a row, a few alternatives per step, a time budget). "Nothing better was found" does not show that no better form exists.
An identity that matches but whose conditions are not provable from your assumptions is reported with the unmet conditions and never applied.
Symbols are complex unless you declare otherwise, so results that need real or positive symbols are left alone until you say so.
If nothing better is found, the input is returned unchanged and the status says so.
Bare function arguments such as `\sin 2x` and inverse notation such as `\sin^{-1}` are rejected as ambiguous.

capabilities.title: Verified Taylor series
capabilities.summary: Expands an expression in one variable about a finite real point, to order 12 at most. The coefficients are re-derived from the original function by a contour-integral estimate (no differentiation), and the remainder is measured to shrink at the claimed order. Both checks must pass or no series is shown.
limits: Only Taylor series about a finite point. A pole or branch point at the point (`1/x`, `\sqrt{x}`, `\ln x` at 0) is "unsupported"; Laurent, Puiseux and asymptotic series are not produced.
Functions with no complex derivative (`|x|`) are unsupported.
The error table is a measurement at a few distances for this expression, not a bound.

capabilities.title: Identity search with applicability checks
capabilities.summary: Retrieval proposes handbook identities that may fit an expression. The engine then matches each pattern, checks its validity conditions against your declared assumptions, rewrites, and verifies the rewrite.
limits: An identity whose conditions cannot be proven from your assumptions is reported, with the unmet conditions, and not applied.
Matches that only work by inventing roots, reciprocals or the imaginary unit are discarded.
Retrieval is keyword and structure based; semantic search is planned.

capabilities.title: Derivations in the workbench
capabilities.summary: Builds a derivation step by step without a language model. Each step is an operation (simplify, differentiate, integrate, Taylor polynomial) or a handbook identity applied to the previous result, and is verified and saved to your account with what produced it and the assumptions in force. You can continue from any earlier step.
limits: A step is carried forward as its text form, which the parser reads back exactly. A result the text parser cannot read (for example one using `erf` or `Piecewise`) is shown but cannot be continued.

An identity is offered only when the engine reports it applicable (conditions proven from your assumptions); applying it recomputes and re-verifies the rewrite on the server. Handbook entries that are only stated are never applied.
If you edit a carried-forward result, the next step is recorded as a new input, not a continuation.

examples.title: Applying a handbook identity as a step
checks: symbolic zero test not established; numeric check agreed at 20 of 20 points
notes: In the workbench this is the Apply button next to an applicable identity; it appears only after the assumptions make the identity applicable.

capabilities.title: Substituting relations
capabilities.summary: Replaces the left side of a relation you supply by its right side, one relation at a time, and records each replacement as a step with the relation it used. The relations are your premises: Minerva checks that the replacement reproduces the original expression, not that your relation is true, so a result that depends on them is shown as holding given them. If the result also holds without them, it says so.
limits: At most four relations, applied once each in the order you give. If another order would give a different result, or the relations rewrite each other, the request is refused until you say whether to apply them in the order listed or all at once; Minerva never picks one.

A relation that can never hold (`x = x + 1`) or relates only numbers is refused. A relation used as a commutation rule (`AB - BA = 1`) is not applied, because only patterns that occur in the expression are replaced.
Replacement finds the occurrences SymPy recognises; a pattern that does not occur leaves the expression unchanged.
The input must be an expression (not an equation). Noncommuting symbols are supported for polynomial expressions, and the order of their factors is kept.
Where a cancelled denominator excludes a point, the result states it (`x \neq 0`).

capabilities.title: Changing one part of an expression
capabilities.summary: Applies one move to one part of an expression and leaves the rest alone: expand, factor, cancel, simplify, collect terms by chosen variables or powers, or a handbook identity. You choose the part from a list the server makes (or type it); if it occurs more than once you choose the occurrence. The whole expression before and after is verified, and an identity whose conditions are not provable from your assumptions is reported and not applied.
limits: A part is chosen for one exact expression; if the expression has changed, the choice is refused as stale and never applied somewhere else.
An identity is matched against the chosen part alone, with the same filters as everywhere else (no invented roots, reciprocals or the imaginary unit).

Collect works on symbols and parts of the expression, at most four, and by commuting ones for noncommuting expressions. For noncommuting symbols only expand and collect are supported, on polynomial expressions; every other operation reports that it does not support them.
Verification is numerical, and symbolic where SymPy finds a zero; for noncommuting symbols random matrices sized from the degree are used.

capabilities.title: Solving an equation for one variable
capabilities.summary: Isolates a variable in an equation and lists every solution with the conditions it needs: parameters that must not vanish, values the equation itself excludes, and the parameter values where it degenerates. Polynomial and rational equations are solved in closed form where one exists; a variable that occurs once inside powers, roots, exp and log is solved by undoing each operation, one recorded step at a time. Every solution is substituted back into your equation, and a separate check shows that none was dropped.
limits: Solutions are over the complex numbers. Assumptions on the unknown (real, positive) are not used to choose among them, and the result says so; a logarithm or an exponential gives a family with an integer k_1.

Supported are linear and quadratic factors with symbolic coefficients, cubic and quartic factors with rational coefficients, and one occurrence of the unknown inside sums, products, powers, principal roots, exp and log (a base is accepted only if known positive). Periodic inverses (sin, cos), absolute values, symbolic exponents of the unknown, systems of equations and symbolic polynomials of degree three or more are unsupported, and no partial answer is given.
A root that makes a denominator zero is removed, and a principal root can make a candidate extraneous (the equation √x = -2 has no solution). An equation with no solution is reported as such.
Noncommuting symbols are not supported here.

capabilities.title: Lagrangian mechanics
capabilities.summary: From a Lagrangian and its coordinates, derives the Euler–Lagrange equations, momenta and accelerations, and finds constants of motion by cyclic coordinates, time translation and rotations of coordinate pairs. Each constant is verified: its time derivative is zero on the equations of motion.
limits: Symmetries that hold only up to a total time derivative (Galilean boosts) are not searched for, and the result says so. Hidden symmetries such as the Runge–Lenz vector are not found here; the separate search for more constants of motion looks for them in a declared family.

capabilities.title: Search for hidden constants of motion
capabilities.summary: Looks for constants of motion beyond cyclic coordinates, energy and rotations, such as the Runge–Lenz vector of the Kepler problem. It solves exactly for every combination of functions of the coordinates (powers, and cos and sin of coordinates you declare to be angles) times velocity monomials of a chosen degree whose time derivative vanishes on the equations of motion. Only constants that pass the same verification as the others are shown, and the known ones and their products are left out of the count.
limits: It searches one declared family and says which. Finding nothing proves nothing outside that family.
Time-dependent Lagrangians, accelerations with square roots or other non-rational functions, and more than three coordinates are refused.
The family is capped (500 unknown coefficients); a bigger one is reported as a resource limit.
Naming a constant (for example as the Runge–Lenz vector) is a recognition the model may offer, not something the search proves.

capabilities.title: Citable handbook
capabilities.summary: Handbook entries state identities, integrals, series, special functions and physical equations in original wording and cite sources by locator only. Each entry is verified at a declared level, or labelled "stated" when it is a literature record that is never applied.
limits: Entries recorded from the literature ("stated") carry no rule and are never used to rewrite anything.
Coverage is limited and growing; quantum field theory is stated entries only.

capabilities.title: Chat with a model you host
capabilities.summary: A conversation in which a language model plans, asks and explains, and calls the tools above. It runs only when you connect a model, such as one served by Ollama; it is off by default.
limits: The model never computes and never decides correctness. Formulas it writes that no tool produced in the conversation are shown as unchecked. Equations it writes are called false only when the sides differ by a constant; definitions, coordinate changes and equations of motion are not identities, stay unchecked, and are judged only against definitions stated earlier in the conversation.
How well it chooses tools depends on the model, and no model tried so far passes every evaluation case. See docs/model-evaluation.md.
Only Ollama-compatible hosts are supported.

capabilities.summary: Attach a photo or screenshot of an equation in the chat. A vision model you host transcribes it to LaTeX, you confirm or correct the transcription, and Minerva's strict parser shows how it reads each formula before anything is computed. The model only transcribes; it never solves, simplifies or decides anything about the image.
limits: A transcription can be wrong, which is why you confirm it before it is used. Only what the parser accepts from the confirmed text is passed on to the tools.
Ambiguous notation is refused exactly as typed input is, for example `\sin 2x`.
Images are never stored or logged, and are limited in size to PNG, JPEG or WebP files.
It needs a vision-capable model on the Ollama-compatible host you connect.

examples.title: A transcribed equation, read by the strict parser
checks: strict parser: the formula is parsed, never simplified or evaluated
notes: This is the step after the vision model and your confirmation: the confirmed LaTeX is read by the same parser as typed input, and nothing is simplified.
